A.explanation: Too small. It results from using a wrong distance for the weight of the rule, such as measuring from the 0 cm end instead of from the pivot.

B.explanation: Too small. It results from an error in the moment arms, for example using $34.0 - 4.0$ incorrectly or swapping the two sides of the pivot.

C.explanation: Balances moments about the pivot: $64 \times 30.0 = m \times 16.0$, giving $m = 120 \text{ g}$.

D.explanation: Too large. It is close to using the full $34.0 \text{ cm}$ or $50.0 \text{ cm}$ length as a moment arm instead of the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass.

hints: Notice the three positions on the rule: the $64 \text{ g}$ mass at $4.0 \text{ cm}$, the pivot at $34.0 \text{ cm}$, and the centre of mass of the uniform rule at $50.0 \text{ cm}$.
Connect balance to the principle of moments about the $34.0 \text{ cm}$ pivot: anticlockwise moment from the $64 \text{ g}$ mass equals clockwise moment from the weight of the rule.
Calculate the two perpendicular distances from the pivot, $34.0 - 4.0$ and $50.0 - 34.0$, then set $m \times 16.0 = 64 \times 30.0$ with masses in $\text{g}$ and distances in $\text{cm}$.
walkthrough: The weight of a uniform metre rule acts at its midpoint, so at the $50.0 \text{ cm}$ mark, while the pivot is at $34.0 \text{ cm}$ and the added mass is at $4.0 \text{ cm}$.
Distance of $64 \text{ g}$ mass to the left of the pivot is $34.0 - 4.0 = 30.0 \text{ cm}$. Distance of the centre of mass to the right of the pivot is $50.0 - 34.0 = 16.0 \text{ cm}$.
For balance the sum of moments about the pivot is zero, so clockwise moment due to rule equals anticlockwise moment due to $64 \text{ g}$ mass.
Let mass of rule be $m$. Using $\text{moment} = \text{force} \times \text{distance}$ and cancelling $g$: $m \times 16.0 = 64 \times 30.0$.
Solve: $m = 64 \times 30.0 / 16.0 = 1920 / 16.0 = 120 \text{ g}$. Units check as $\text{g} \times \text{cm}$ on both sides. This is option C.
